claim: Many primate genes produce circular RNAs (circRNAs).
source: Many primate genes produce circular RNAs (circRNAs).
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript showing circRNA expression across multiple primate species.

claim: Within 3 million years circRNA expression profiles diverged such that they are more related to species identity than organ type.
source: By comparing tissue-specific transcriptomes across over 70 million years of primate evolution, we identify that within 3 million years circRNA expression profiles diverged such that they are more related to species identity than organ type.
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, which demonstrate species-specific clustering of circRNA expression rather than tissue-specific clustering.

claim: A subset of circRNAs show conserved neural expression across tens of millions of years of evolution.
source: However, our analysis also revealed a subset of circRNAs with conserved neural expression across tens of millions of years of evolution.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1D showing tissue-dominated clustering across brain samples and the identification of ~773 conserved circRNAs.

claim: The downstream intron of conserved circRNAs displays a dramatic lengthening during evolution due to the insertion of novel retrotransposons.
source: By comparing to species-specific circRNAs, we identified that the downstream intron of the conserved circRNAs display a dramatic lengthening during evolution due to the insertion of novel retrotransposons.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C and 4D showing increased intron length and novel transposon insertion in conserved circRNAs compared to species-specific circRNAs.

claim: Increased biological complexity has arisen in part by the dynamic generation of unique cell-specific transcriptomes.
source: Through decades of research, it has been shown that increased biological complexity has arisen in part by the dynamic generation of unique cell-specific transcriptomes, and as a consequence of the highly versatile programs of gene expression (Brawand et al., 2011; Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gene expression is highly conserved between the same tissues in different species.
source: However, studies of tissues across distant animal lineages have shown that gene expression is highly conserved between the same tissues in different species (Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012; Brawand et al., 2011; Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2019; Merkin et al., 2012; Reyes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and is confirmed by the data in Figure 1B showing tissue-specific clustering of gene expression.

claim: Gene expression alone is unlikely to explain the heterogeneous expansion in complexity across vertebrate evolution.
source: Hence, gene expression alone is unlikely to explain the heterogeneous expansion in complexity (as defined by the number of cell types) across vertebrate evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gene expression is conserved across species despite differences in complexity.

claim: Post-transcriptional mechanisms capable of greatly expanding transcriptomic diversity underlie advances in biological complexity.
source: Instead, it is becoming increasingly evident that the plethora of post-transcriptional mechanisms (Cheetham et al., 2020; Fiszbein et al., 2019; Gueroussov et al., 2017; Ha et al., 2018; Ha et al., 2021; Mattick, 2018) capable of greatly expanding transcriptomic diversity also underlies these advances.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on post-transcriptional mechanisms.

claim: CircRNAs can regulate protein localization.
source: These RNAs can regulate protein localization (Liu et al., 2019), miRNA functionality (Piwecka et al., 2017), and a range of other processes (Li et al., 2018a; Gokool et al., 2020a), enabling increased regulatory complexity, especially in the immune and nervous systems (Gokool et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Piwecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: CircRNAs can regulate miRNA functionality.
source: These RNAs can regulate protein localization (Liu et al., 2019), miRNA functionality (Piwecka et al., 2017), and a range of other processes (Li et al., 2018a; Gokool et al., 2020a), enabling increased regulatory complexity, especially in the immune and nervous systems (Gokool et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Piwecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piwecka et al., 2017.

claim: CircRNAs enable increased regulatory complexity, especially in the immune and nervous systems.
source: These RNAs can regulate protein localization (Liu et al., 2019), miRNA functionality (Piwecka et al., 2017), and a range of other processes (Li et al., 2018a; Gokool et al., 2020a), enabling increased regulatory complexity, especially in the immune and nervous systems (Gokool et al., 2020b; Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Piwecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CircRNAs form by back-splicing whereby an exon's 3′-splice site is ligated to an upstream 5′-splice site forming a closed circRNA transcript.
source: CircRNAs form by back-splicing whereby an exon's 3′-splice site is ligated to an upstream 5′-splice site forming a closed circRNA transcript (Barrett et al., 2015; Starke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Back-splicing occurs both co- and post-transcriptionally.
source: Back-splicing occurs both co- and post-transcriptionally and is facilitated by inverted repeat elements that promote complementarity between adjacent introns favoring circRNA formation over linear splicing (Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Liang and Wilusz, 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Back-splicing is facilitated by inverted repeat elements that promote complementarity between adjacent introns favoring circRNA formation over linear splicing.
source: Back-splicing occurs both co- and post-transcriptionally and is facilitated by inverted repeat elements that promote complementarity between adjacent introns favoring circRNA formation over linear splicing (Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Liang and Wilusz, 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and is confirmed by the data in Figure 3D showing enrichment of inverted repeat elements.

claim: RNA-RNA interactions can be facilitated by RNA-binding proteins, such as Quaking, that help stabilize the hair-pin structure promoting circRNA formation.
source: These RNA-RNA interactions can be facilitated by RNA-binding proteins, such as Quaking (Conn et al., 2015), that help stabilize the hair-pin structure promoting circRNA formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Conn et al., 2015.

claim: The production of circRNAs can arise due to the perturbed expression of trans-factors and the inhibition of the core splicing machinery.
source: The production of circRNAs can also arise due to the perturbed expression of trans-factors and the inhibition of the core splicing machinery (Aktaş et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spuriously produced circRNAs are maintained as their circular shape protects them from the activity of cellular exonucleases.
source: These spuriously produced circRNAs are maintained as their circular shape protects them from the activity of cellular exonucleases (Gokool et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about circRNA stability.

claim: The variable usage of cis-regulatory elements in exons and flanking introns can be selected to promote circRNA expression in a cell-type, condition- or species-specific manner.
source: In contrast, the variable usage of cis-regulatory elements in exons and flanking introns can be selected to promote circRNA expression in a cell-type, condition- or species-specific manner (Irimia and Blencowe, 2012; Nilsen and Graveley, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study analyzed transcriptomic data from nine tissues from eight primate species.
source: To address the outstanding questions about the conservation and functional importance of circRNAs, we collected transcriptomic (RNA-seq) data (Peng et al., 2015; Pipes et al., 2013) from across nine tissues from eight primate species, consisting of three old-world monkeys, two hominoids, two new-world monkeys, and one prosimian (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: The species studied span from <3 million years to >70 million years of evolutionary divergence.
source: These species were chosen on the basis of the quality of their genomes and their close evolutionary relationships enabling the evaluation of transcriptome changes between species ranging from <3 million years to >70 million years (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1A showing divergence times.

claim: Gene expression shows a clear pattern of tissue-specific conservation across primate species.
source: In agreement with previous results (Brawand et al., 2011; Merkin et al., 2012; Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012; Reyes et al., 2013) from analysis across vertebrate species, a clear pattern emerged of tissue-specific conservation of gene expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1B showing tissue-specific clustering of gene expression.

claim: Most tissues possess a tissue-specific gene expression signature such that a liver-specific gene in chimp will likely also be liver-specific in lemur.
source: This pattern suggests that most tissues possess a tissue-specific gene expression signature such that, for example, a liver-specific gene in chimp will likely also be liver-specific in lemur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific clustering pattern observed in Figure 1B.

claim: In contrast to gene expression, circRNA expression is segregated by species.
source: However, in contrast to gene expression, circRNA expression is segregated by species (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing species-specific clustering of circRNA expression.

claim: Approximately 67% of circRNAs are species-specific with no orthologous circRNAs in other species.
source: This suggests that despite all the exons studied being conserved across primates the majority of circRNAs showed species-specific expression with no orthologous circRNAs in other species (Figure 1C, ~67% are species-specific, n = 11,201).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Conserved circRNAs show tissue-dominated clustering across all types of brain samples.
source: In this analysis, more complex patterns of circRNA conservation emerged with tissue-dominated clustering observed across all types of brain samples (Figure 1D) in line with previous observations (Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015; Venø et al., 2015; You et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1D and citations to previous research.

claim: For non-brain tissues, circRNAs showed primarily species-specific clustering.
source: In contrast, for all other tissues circRNAs showed primarily species-specific clustering.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: Genes containing conserved and species-specific circRNAs did not show significant differences in gene expression.
source: A comparison of genes containing conserved and species-specific circRNAs did not show any significant differences (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B, p=0.584 Wilcoxon rank-sum test), suggesting that differences between these subgroups are not driven by gene expression differences.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: Genes containing conserved circRNAs neither displayed neural-specific gene expression nor neural-specific alternative splicing changes.
source: Interestingly, genes containing conserved circRNAs neither displayed neural-specific gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) or neural-specific alternative splicing changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: CircRNA conservation and expression is independent of gene expression and alternative splicing regulatory layers.
source: This suggests that circRNA conservation and expression is independent of these regulatory layers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that conserved circRNAs do not show neural-specific gene expression or alternative splicing patterns.

claim: Many orthologous genes consistently express circRNAs even if the precise BSJ is not conserved.
source: Many orthologous genes consistently express circRNAs even if the precise BSJ is not conserved (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1C showing conservation at the gene level.

claim: A median of 10 circRNAs are detected per gene across tissues.
source: This phenomenon persisted across species with a median of 10 circRNAs detected per gene across tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CircRNA production only occurred in 20.4% of orthologous expressed genes.
source: However, this circRNA production only occurred in a limited number of expressed genes (20.4% of orthologous expressed genes).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the dataset.

claim: Certain genomic areas are circRNA factories that are prone to produce large numbers of lowly expressed circRNAs.
source: This suggests that certain genomic areas are circRNA factories that are prone to produce large numbers of lowly expressed circRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some genes produce many circRNAs.

claim: A core set of circRNAs show conserved tissue-specific patterns across neural tissues.
source: These observations suggest that a core set of circRNAs show conserved tissue-specific patterns across neural tissues.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: The great prevalence of circRNAs showing species-specific expression indicates that the cis-regulatory or trans-regulatory environments may differ between even very closely related species.
source: However, the great prevalence of circRNAs showing species-specific expression indicates that the cis-regulatory or trans-regulatory environments may differ between even very closely related species to promote the species-specific production of circRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of species-specific circRNA expression.

claim: Several hundred circRNAs exhibit highly conserved circRNA expression.
source: Our analysis (Figure 2A) reveals clear subsets of several hundred circRNAs exhibiting highly conserved circRNA expression.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CircRNA expression can be conserved for tens of millions of years.
source: The circRNA ERC1 and many other examples from our data (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) demonstrate that circRNA expression can be conserved for tens of millions of years.
evidence: This is supported by examples shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Over 70% of conserved circRNAs show consistent tissue expression across 30 million years of evolution.
source: Initial analysis of conserved circRNAs revealed enrichment within neural tissues with over 70% showing consistent tissue expression across 30 million years of evolution (Supplementary file 2), in line with previous observations (Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015; Venø et al., 2015; You et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Supplementary file 2 and citations to previous research.

claim: Conserved circRNAs display increased inclusion rates compared to species-specific circRNAs.
source: Analysis of expression levels revealed no clear trends for increased expression of conserved circRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, p<0.187, Wilcoxon rank-sum test vs. species-specific); however, these circRNAs did display increased inclusion rates or increased circRNA expression as compared to linear isoform (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, p=3.38 × 10⁻74, Wilcoxon rank-sum test vs. species-specific).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Circularization increased with the conservation age of the circRNA.
source: Furthermore, this inclusion (or circularization) increased with the conservation age of the circRNA (Figure 2E, p=8.07 × 10–19, Wilcoxon rank-sum test of hominoids vs. species-specific [human-specific]; p=2.14 × 10–06, Wilcoxon rank-sum test of hominoids vs. shared until new-world monkeys).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Over time conserved circRNAs are increasingly influencing the transcriptomic abundance of the linear isoform and the protein abundance of the gene.
source: This suggests that over time these circRNAs are increasingly influencing the transcriptomic abundance of the linear isoform and the protein abundance of the gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that circularization increases with conservation age.

claim: Conserved circRNAs contain fewer exons than species-specific circRNAs.
source: Analysis of the exonic structure of conserved circRNAs showed that conserved circRNAs contain fewer exons (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, p = 2.23 × 10–20, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) with a significant enrichment to contain 2–3 exons (p-value = 4.17 × 10–08, Fisher's exact test), which is in line with observations from previous studies (Ragan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, and is consistent with previous research.

claim: Conserved circRNAs rarely overlap with other circRNAs displaying back-splicing at unique 5′- and 3′-splice sites.
source: Conserved circRNAs also rarely overlap with other circRNAs (Figure 2G, p=4.08 × 10–64, Fisher's exact test; see Materials and methods) displaying back-splicing at unique 5′- and 3′-splice sites.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There is tight control of the number of exons within a circRNA and the BSJs used in conserved circRNAs.
source: This indicates a tight control of the number of exons within a circRNA and the BSJs used.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that conserved circRNAs have fewer exons and unique splice sites.

claim: A logistic regression model achieved a high average true-positive rate of 86.7% for distinguishing conserved circRNAs from background circRNAs.
source: After initially training our model on a subset of conserved and background circRNAs (80%), we next assessed its performance on the rest of 20% cirRNAs and observed a high average true-positive rate of 86.7% (AUC, area under the receiver operating characteristic [ROC] curve; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) for a model including 24 variables selected by feature analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A core set of 24 cis- and trans-regulatory features are enriched within the conserved formation of circRNAs.
source: This identifies a core set of 24 cis- and trans-regulatory features enriched within the conserved formation of circRNAs compared to our background set of introns (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the feature importance analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Features associated with conserved circRNAs include inverted repeat Alu elements and exon and intron length.
source: This includes multiple features previously associated with conserved circRNAs, such as inverted repeat Alu elements (Jeck et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014), as well as exon and intron length (Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the feature analysis in Figure 3A and B and citations to previous research.

claim: A logistic regression model achieved a true-positive rate of 65.4% for distinguishing conserved from species-specific circRNAs.
source: As expected, our model distinguished these categories less efficiently but was still able to achieve a true-positive rate of 65.4% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) driven by 12 features.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Conserved circRNAs show depletion of nucleosomes in the downstream intron compared to species-specific circRNAs.
source: Notable among these features was the depletion of nucleosomes in the downstream intron of the circRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, 1.57 × 10–03, Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon rank-sum test [BH-Wilcox] vs. species-specific) and the presence of a more defined 3′-splice site at the final exon (p=2.04 × 10–03, BH-Wilcox vs. species-specific).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Introns adjacent to conserved circRNAs exhibited a significant enrichment for repeat elements, in particular inverted-repeat L1 and AluJ retrotransposons.
source: Introns adjacent to conserved circRNAs also exhibited a significant enrichment for repeat elements (Figure 3D, all p<1 × 10–5, BH-Wilcox vs. species-specific) in particular inverted-repeat L1 and AluJ retrotransposons (:Figure 3D, L1: p<1.22 × 10–23| AluJ: p<1.48 × 10–18, BH-Wilcox).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In species-specific circRNA, the adjacent downstream intron has a median length of 4624 nucleotides whilst in conserved circRNA the median is almost twice as long at 9923 nucleotides.
source: In species-specific circRNA, this adjacent downstream intron has a median length of 4624 nucleotides whilst in conserved circRNA the median is almost twice as long at 9923 nucleotides (Figure 4B, p<1.07 × 10–35, BH-Wilcox).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Over 90% of features overlapped between the models comparing conserved vs. background and conserved vs. species-specific circRNAs.
source: Finally, when comparing the major drivers of both models, we noticed over 90% (11/12) of features overlapped between the models.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the feature analysis results.

claim: Conserved circRNAs are an extreme continuum of species-specific circRNAs.
source: This suggests that conserved circRNAs are an extreme continuum of species-specific circRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that features overlap between the two models.

claim: Understanding the processes contributing to circRNA conservation may also provide insight into the genesis of circRNAs across species.
source: Therefore, understanding the processes contributing to circRNA conservation may also provide insight into the genesis of circRNAs across species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that conserved circRNAs are an extreme continuum of species-specific circRNAs.

claim: The human introns downstream of all identified circRNAs show an almost fourfold expansion compared to background dataset of introns within circRNA containing genes.
source: In contrast to orthologous lemur introns, the human introns downstream of all identified circRNAs shows an almost fourfold expansion compared to background dataset of introns within circRNA containing genes (Figure 4C, p<3.84 × 10–23, Wilcoxon rank-sum) and the upstream adjacent intron (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, p<1.02 × 10–10, Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Conserved circRNAs display an almost twofold greater lengthening than species-specific circRNAs.
source: This difference is even greater in conserved circRNA, which display an almost twofold greater lengthening than species-specific circRNAs (or eightfold over background; Figure 4C, p<3.84 × 10–06, Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expansion of the intron downstream of the circRNA may increase the proportion of back-splicing events increasing the likelihood of circRNA conservation.
source: These observations suggest that the expansion of the intron downstream of the circRNA may increase the proportion of back-splicing events increasing the likelihood of circRNA conservation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased intron length in conserved circRNAs.

claim: The insertion of novel transposons occurs at almost double the frequency in introns associated with conserved circRNAs.
source: This analysis revealed the insertion of novel transposons at almost double the frequency in introns associated with conserved circRNAs (Figure 4D, p<5.48 × 10–06, Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in intron length is driven by the novel insertion of AluJ and L1 elements.
source: Further evaluation of the retrotransposons revealed that this increase in length is driven by the novel insertion of AluJ and L1 elements (Figure 4E, AluJ: p<0.018; L1: p<1.73 × 10–04, Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Retrotransposition is potentially facilitated by the depletion of nucleosome occupancy in these introns compared to other human introns.
source: This retrotransposition is potentially facilitated by the depletion of nucleosome occupancy in these introns compared to other human introns (Figure 3B, p<1.15 × 10–07, BH-Wilcox).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of nucleosome depletion.

claim: Young transposons play a role in creating longer intronic regions, which increases the time for RNA polymerase II to reach next canonical splice site and therefore increases likelihood of back-junction splicing to occur.
source: Together, this argues for the role of young transposons in creating longer intronic regions, which increases the time for RNA polymerase II to reach next canonical splice site and therefore increases likelihood of back-junction splicing to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations of transposon insertion and intron lengthening.

claim: The evolution of circRNAs has been previously studied across extensive evolutionary time revealing poor conservation for the majority of circRNAs.
source: The evolution of circRNAs has been previously studied across extensive evolutionary time revealing poor conservation for the majority of circRNAs (Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015; Venø et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study's approach is unique as it focuses on the conservation of circRNAs in very closely related species.
source: Our approach is unique as it focuses on the conservation of circRNAs in very closely related species, enabling us to account for the rapid evolution of these RNAs.
evidence: This describes the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: There is extensive variation in the production of the vast majority of circRNAs between species.
source: Firstly, we observe extensive variation in the production of the vast majority of circRNAs between species.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing species-specific circRNA expression.

claim: CircRNAs are often expressed within the same orthologous genes even if BSJ is not conserved.
source: With circRNAs often expressed within the same orthologous genes even if BSJ is not conserved.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1C.

claim: A core set of over 700 circRNAs are conserved across millions of years of evolution.
source: Conversely, we identify a core set of over 700 circRNAs that are conserved across millions of years of evolution.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of ~773 conserved circRNAs.

claim: Conserved circRNAs have higher inclusion rates and show increased inclusion across evolutionary age.
source: These circRNAs have higher inclusion rates and show increased inclusion across evolutionary age.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2E.

claim: Both conserved and species-specific circRNAs are related in the cis- and trans-regulatory features that correlate with circRNA formation.
source: Both groups are related in the cis- and trans-regulatory features that correlate with circRNA formation such as evidence of recent transposons insertion and extended adjacent introns (Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the feature analysis in Figure 3 and citations to previous research.

claim: The majority of circRNAs identified arose from the same gene locus (alternative circularization).
source: In line with previous work, the majority of circRNAs identified arose from the same gene locus (alternative circularization) (Burd et al., 2010; Jeck et al., 2013; Salzman et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014); however, we identify that this phenomenon is largely limited to species-specific circRNAs and disappears in the conserved group.
evidence: This is supported by the data and citations to previous research.

claim: The adjacent introns of circRNAs are significantly longer with inverted Alu repeats.
source: Similarly, we identify that the adjacent introns of circRNAs are significantly longer with inverted Alu repeats (Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2017); however, only in the conserved group do we observe a bias towards lengthening of the downstream adjacent intron with inverted L1 repeats dominating.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4 and citations to previous research.

claim: Conserved circRNAs do not have higher expression but have greater relative expression compared to linear transcript with this ratio increasing with the evolutionary age of the circRNA.
source: Finally, in contrast to previous work, we do not identify that conserved circRNAs are more strongly expressed but instead that conserved circRNAs have greater relative expression compared to linear transcript with this ratio increasing with the evolutionary age of the circRNA.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2.

claim: The decreased diversity of conserved circRNA production and increased relative expression is in line with data from linear splicing and suggests circRNA selection is occurring.
source: This decreased diversity of conserved circRNA production and increased relative expression is in line with data from linear splicing (Baek and Green, 2005; Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012; Gueroussov et al., 2017; Irimia et al., 2009; Merkin et al., 2012) and suggests circRNA selection is occurring.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations and citations to previous research on linear splicing.

claim: The formation of Alu exons is suppressed by the nuclear ribonucleoprotein HNRNPC.
source: For example, the formation of Alu exons is suppressed by the nuclear ribonucleoprotein HNRNPC (Zarnack et al., 2013) and the nuclear helicase DHX9 binds to inverted repeat Alu elements to suppress circRNA formation (Aktaş et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nuclear helicase DHX9 binds to inverted repeat Alu elements to suppress circRNA formation.
source: For example, the formation of Alu exons is suppressed by the nuclear ribonucleoprotein HNRNPC (Zarnack et al., 2013) and the nuclear helicase DHX9 binds to inverted repeat Alu elements to suppress circRNA formation (Aktaş et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aktaş et al., 2017.

claim: Over time, retrotransposon inclusions can promote novel functionality enabling the creation of tissue-specific exons, miRNAs, and promoter regions.
source: Over time though, in selected examples, these inclusions can promote novel functionality (Attig et al., 2016; Attig et al., 2018; Avgan et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2011), enabling the creation of tissue-specific exons (Attig et al., 2018), miRNAs (Gu et al., 2009; Spengler et al., 2014), and promoter regions (Li et al., 2018a; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CircRNAs are undergoing a selection race with the recent insertion of multiple retrotransposons promoting increased circRNA production that in some cases stabilizes over time.
source: Our results suggest that circRNAs are undergoing a similar selection race with the recent insertion of multiple retrotransposons promoting increased circRNA production that in some cases stabilizes over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations of transposon insertion and circRNA conservation.

claim: The production of a large number of circRNAs in itself can be functional, such as in the immune system where circRNAs sequester RNA-binding proteins.
source: It is important to note though that the production of a large number of circRNAs in itself can be functional (Liu et al., 2019). For example, in the immune system a wide diversity of circRNAs are produced to sequester-specific RNA-binding proteins. These proteins are released upon viral infection to inhibit translation of viral RNA (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The results support a kinetic model for circRNA function whereby trans-factors promote spliceosome recruitment to the final exon and the very long downstream introns extend the time window for back-splicing to occur.
source: Our results support a kinetic model (Schor et al., 2013) for circRNA function whereby trans-factors promote spliceosome recruitment to the final exon and the very long downstream introns extend the time window for back-splicing to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations and citation to Schor et al., 2013.

claim: The extension of the final intron increases the likelihood of circRNA formation in time and space.
source: The extension of the final intron therefore increases the likelihood of circRNA formation in time and space. Spatially by introducing new retrotransposons, which facilitates RNA-RNA duplex formation (Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017; Liang and Wilusz, 2014) to orientate the splice sites in close proximity and temporary by increasing the intron length, it expands the time window for such an event to occur (Veloso et al., 2014), which acts independent of the rate of RNA polymerase II across the gene body (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations and citations to previous research.

claim: This model conforms with previous observations of enrichment of inverted repeat Alu elements and of long introns surrounding circRNAs.
source: This model conforms with the previous observations of enrichment of inverted repeat Alu elements and of long introns surrounding circRNAs (Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Dong et al., 2017; Ivanov et al., 2015; Jeck et al., 2013; Liang and Wilusz, 2014; Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The conservation of circRNAs could be a result of increasing the probability for back-splicing to occur rather than evidence of functionality.
source: The conservation of circRNAs we observe could therefore just be a result of increasing the probability for such an event to occur rather than evidence of functionality.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the results.

claim: CircRNAs represent an extreme example of a trend in post-transcriptional regulation whereby low leaky expression creates a pool of possible novel substrates.

claim: Whippet has a low false positive rate (<2%).
source: Our analysis of both simulated and collected RNA-seq data found that Whippet has a low false positive rate (<2%, see Materials and methods for details), which is in line with other methods (Szabo et al., 2015, Gokool et al., 2020a), a high rate of circRNA identification even at low read depths (~90%; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) and is faster (~69 min) with less computational overhead (<3 GB of memory on a single core) than other highly cited circRNA algorithms we compared with (CIRCexplorer3 [Ma et al., 2019], CIRIquant [Zhang et al., 2020], and find_circ [Memczak et al., 2013]; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
